t: Reverse Letters Then Special Characters in a String
o:
Letters keep their positions but appear in reverse order among themselves; likewise special characters keep their positions but reverse among themselves. With length ≤ 100, any straightforward simulation works.

Example 1: letters ')ebc#da@f(' → ['e','b','c','d','a','f'] reversed → place back into letter slots giving ')fad#cb@e(', then specials [')','#','@','('] reversed fill the special slots producing '(fad@cb#e)'. Example 3 shows the degenerate all-special case, which is just a full string reversal.
k: Positions are fixed; only the order within each character class changes.

a.i: Collect letters and specials separately, reverse each list, then walk the original string and overwrite each slot from the corresponding reversed list. This directly mirrors the two-step operation described in the statement.
s: Split s into a letters list and a specials list, each reversed.
Scan the original positions: replace letter slots from the reversed letters list, special slots from the reversed specials list.
a.t: O(n) — three linear passes over a string of length ≤ 100

a.i: Swap letters symmetrically with two pointers skipping specials, then reset and do the same for specials. This avoids auxiliary lists and is the classic 'reverse only letters' pattern applied twice.
s: Pointer i from left, j from right: advance until both sit on letters, swap, move inward.
Reset pointers and repeat the same procedure for special characters.
a.t: O(n) — each pointer sweep visits every character once per phase
a.sp: O(n) for the char array (O(1) extra in languages with mutable strings)

w: Either approach is fine at this size; the two-pointer version generalizes to huge inputs with O(1) extra space. Pitfalls: applying the reversal to the whole string instead of per-class, or reversing classes in the wrong order (here order does not matter since the classes occupy disjoint slots). Follow-up: reverse only letters (LeetCode 917) is the special case with no second phase.
